title: Oil Markets Weigh Iran's Hormuz Mine Claim Before Sunday's Futures Open
dek: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says two tankers hit mines south of the strait, a claim no second source has confirmed. Brent settled at $95.84 Friday, so Sunday's futures open is the first test.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Map of the Strait of Hormuz connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman

keyPoints: The IRGC Navy says two tankers struck naval mines and caught fire south of the Strait of Hormuz (Anadolu; Tasnim). CBS News carried the Guards' figure as three tankers and said the strikes could not be verified.
Brent settled at $95.84 and WTI at $88.56 on Friday, Nov. 13, their second straight weekly decline (CNBC, citing Reuters).
Gulf of Oman to China VLCC rates eased to about 776 Worldscale from 841 but remain near record levels (Baltic Exchange data via PipeXchange, Nov. 4).
Chevron closed Friday at $219.89 (FinWire). Lockheed Martin ($604.09) and Northrop Grumman ($549.22) closed Nov. 12 (Investorideas via Alphio).
Dated catalysts: Sunday futures reopen at 6 p.m. ET; APEC in Shenzhen Nov. 18-19; Putin-Xi-Trump meeting Nov. 19; FOMC Dec. 9.
body:
## What the Revolutionary Guard said

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said that two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire south of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Anadolu's Sunday morning briefing. The force said the ships were trying to pass along an unauthorized route with their navigation and automatic identification systems switched off, and that the blasts set off large fires aboard both vessels. Tasnim, an Iranian outlet, carried a version of the same statement issued Saturday night, and said two other tankers that had planned covert passage turned back after warnings from the Guards' traffic control center.

The counts do not agree. Anadolu and Tasnim describe two tankers. CBS News' live blog carried the Guards' statement as three tankers on fire and said the strikes could not be verified. The Guards did not name the ships.

The claim fits a pattern. The IRGC Navy said on Wednesday night that two supertankers were disabled by explosions after hitting mines, CNBC reported on Nov. 12. Anadolu carried a separate IRGC statement from Friday, Nov. 13, about two tankers hitting mines in the same waterway. Iran's military also said four tankers were hit on Thursday. Reuters said it could not immediately verify those accounts, as CNBC reported on Nov. 13.

## Who has confirmed it

No independent confirmation appeared in the sources checked for this piece. We found no statement about Sunday's incident from a shipowner, flag state, insurer or the US military. The only sources are the IRGC and the outlets that repeated its statement. Until one of those parties speaks, treat the incident as the Iranian military's claim.

## Where oil started the week

Brent futures settled at $95.84 a barrel on Friday, Nov. 13, up 2 cents. West Texas Intermediate finished at $88.56, down 18 cents, according to CNBC's report on Reuters data. For the week, both benchmarks fell about 2.5%, their second straight weekly decline. In the prior week, Brent and WTI had fallen 16% and 13% (CNBC, Nov. 13).

Those Friday settles are the last verified benchmark prices in this piece. Sunday's first trade, at 6 p.m. ET, is the first to reflect the mine claim. Oil also had a volatile week. Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure and attacks on tankers leaving the Gulf kept a risk premium in the market. Against that, the International Energy Agency reported a rising global surplus, and US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that a deal with Iran was not necessary to end the war (CNBC, Nov. 13).

## What would move prices at Sunday's open

The market will read the claim through two channels. The first is physical supply. The strait is the main route for crude exports from the Gulf producers, so a mined passage raises the risk to barrels leaving the region. The second is shipping cost. Freight for very large crude carriers on the Gulf of Oman to China route fell to about 776 on the Worldscale basis in early November, from 841 the week before. That was the highest reading since the rate was launched this year. Rates remained close to record highs, and ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait kept tanker demand elevated (Baltic Exchange data, via PipeXchange, Nov. 4).

A confirmed strike would likely lift tanker rates and war-risk insurance quickly. An unconfirmed claim is more likely to produce a short spike that fades if no damage is shown, especially while the surplus story is still in play. That is our base case, but confidence is low until a second source confirms the incident.

## Energy and defense equities

Chevron closed Friday at $219.89, up 1.64% (FinWire). A sustained crude premium would support upstream producers, and a fade would undo the gain. We did not verify an Exxon close for this piece.

Defense contractors trade on budget headlines as much as war headlines. Investorideas data showed Lockheed Martin at $604.09 and Northrop Grumman at $549.22 at the Nov. 12 close, with the group drifting lower (Alphio). Defense shares fell after the Nov. 3 midterms, and the Pentagon runs on a stopgap that expires Dec. 11 (Alphio). A mine headline would normally help the group, but the budget calendar may matter more this week.

Tanker equities such as Frontline and DHT Holdings are the most direct listed exposure to freight. We did not verify their Friday closes, so no prices are quoted for them.

## Dated catalysts

- Sunday, 6 p.m. ET: US stock and oil futures reopen, the first market reaction to the IRGC claim.
- Nov. 18-19: APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. The Kremlin says Putin, Xi and Trump will meet on the sidelines on Nov. 19 (Anadolu).
- Dec. 9: FOMC decision. CME FedWatch priced a December hike at 100% (CNBC, Nov. 13).

## What would change the read

A named shipowner, insurer or flag state confirming damage, or a US statement on the strait, would firm up the risk. A quick denial, or reports that the vessels passed the area without incident, would fade it. Friday's settles are the baseline for judging Sunday's move, and Monday's cash session is the first full read.

marketImpact.summary: A confirmed mine strike on tankers would add a supply-risk premium to crude, lift tanker rates and war-risk costs, and support energy names. Unconfirmed, the claim is more likely to produce a short spike than a lasting move, given the surplus story and Friday's weak tape.
